photon-energy-threshold.idea: Each photon must bring enough energy to free an electron.
photon-energy-threshold.explanation: A photon is one packet of light. Higher frequency means more energy per packet; at fixed frequency, greater brightness means more packets. Some photon energy is spent freeing the electron.

example.title: Freeing one electron
steps: One photon brings 3.3088 eV of energy. The material needs 2.20 eV to free an electron.
The fastest freed electron keeps 3.3088 − 2.20 = 1.1088 eV of motion energy.

photon-energy-threshold.equation: maximum motion energy = photon energy − release energy

terms.definition: One packet of light energy.
Electronvolt: a small unit of energy.

photon-momentum-scattering.idea: A photon can give some of its energy to an electron.
photon-momentum-scattering.explanation: When light scatters, it changes direction. For a free electron initially at rest, the outgoing photon can lose energy while the electron gains motion energy; total energy and momentum remain balanced.

example.title: A right-angle scattering
steps: A photon with wavelength 50.0 pm scatters through 90°. Its new wavelength is 52.426 pm.
It loses about 1,148 eV, which becomes the electron’s motion energy.

photon-momentum-scattering.equation: wavelength increase at 90° = h / (electron mass × light speed)

terms.definition: A change in direction caused by an interaction.
Picometre: one trillionth of a metre.
Planck’s constant, which links photon energy to frequency.
One packet of electromagnetic radiation. Visible light and radio waves can both be described in photons.
The distance along a wave from one point to the matching point in the next cycle, such as crest to crest.

lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.2.description: Use rounded m_e≈9.109×10⁻³¹ kg, c≈3.000×10⁸ m/s and Compton wavelength ≈2.426 pm in simple examples.

matter-wavelength.idea: The more momentum a particle has, the shorter its matter wave’s wavelength.
matter-wavelength.explanation: Wavelength is the spacing from one wave crest to the next. Momentum describes motion and its direction. Double the size of a particle’s momentum and its matter wavelength halves. This spacing can affect a pattern made by many detections, even though it does not give the particle’s physical width.

example.title: A moving electron
steps: An electron with motion energy 150 eV has momentum about 6.616 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s.
Dividing Planck’s constant by this momentum gives wavelength about 0.1001 nm.

terms.definition: A quantity that describes directed motion.
Nanometre: one billionth of a metre.
Planck’s constant, about 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds.
The distance along a wave from one point to the matching point in the next cycle, such as crest to crest.

single-event-interference.idea: Many detections reveal a pattern; one detection gives one result.
single-event-interference.explanation: Repeat the same preparation to test its predicted chances. The expected count is a long-run average, so one batch need not match it exactly. The pattern alone does not reveal each particle’s path.

example.title: Counting detections
steps: A region has a 25% chance of receiving each detection. Repeat the experiment independently 400 times.
The expected count is 400 × 0.25 = 100; a batch of 96 can still fit this prediction.

single-event-interference.equation: expected count = number of runs × probability

terms.definition: The average count predicted over many repeated batches.

complex-amplitudes.idea: To predict whether quantum waves will add or cancel, we need more than a list of chances.
complex-amplitudes.explanation: An amplitude is a number with a size and a phase. Think of phase as the direction of an arrow in a calculation. Two arrows of equal size can point together or opposite ways. Add the amplitudes first. For a single possible reading, squaring the size of the result gives its chance when the state is normalized.

example.title: Two amplitudes
steps: Use amplitudes 3/5 and 4i/5, where i² = −1.
Their squared sizes are 9/25 and 16/25. They add to 1.

terms.definition: A number used to calculate quantum chances.
The relative alignment of amplitudes.
The real and imaginary parts of a complex amplitude.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.

lessonCopy.example.steps.2: Their sum is 1, so this coefficient column is normalized. Replacing c₁ by −4i/5 leaves its squared size unchanged but changes the relative phase.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.2.description: Conjugation changes i to −i; i²=−1. The expression c* · c means c* multiplied by c.

born-discrete.idea: A wave number called an amplitude can give the chance of one chosen measurement result.
born-discrete.explanation: First make sure the chances of all the separate outcomes add to one. This is called normalization. Find the size of the amplitude for the outcome you want and multiply that size by itself. A size of one half gives a chance of one quarter.

example.title: Two possible outcomes
steps: Start with amplitudes 1 and 2i. Their squared sizes add to 5.
Divide each amplitude by √5. The outcome chances are then 1/5 and 4/5.

terms.definition: Scaled so the total probability is one.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

continuous-density.idea: Add probability density over a region to find its chance.
continuous-density.explanation: Density tells how tightly probability is packed into space. A high density is not itself a probability; the width of the region also matters.

example.title: A small position interval
steps: A uniform density is 5 per metre within a 0.20 m region.
A 0.030 m piece inside it has chance 5 × 0.030 = 0.15, or 15%.

continuous-density.equation: probability in a region = integral of density across that region

terms.definition: Probability per unit length in this one-dimensional description.
A continuous sum over the region.

lessonCopy.example.steps.0: For a simple probability example, let density be 5 m⁻¹ over a 0.20 m interval and zero elsewhere. Its integral is (5 m⁻¹)(0.20 m)=1.

global-relative-phase.idea: How wave parts line up can change the chance of a measurement result.
global-relative-phase.explanation: Phase marks a wave’s place in its cycle. Picture two arrows whose directions represent the two phases. Turning both by the same amount leaves the size of their sum unchanged. Turning only one changes their relationship, so their sum can grow or shrink.

example.title: Changing one relative sign
steps: Prepare (u₀ + u₁)/√2. A measurement testing that same plus combination succeeds with certainty.
Change only the second sign to minus. The plus amplitudes now cancel, giving zero chance for that outcome.

global-relative-phase.equation: plus-outcome probability = |overlap with the plus state|²

terms.definition: The relative alignment of amplitudes.
Two orthogonal normalized reference states.
The amplitude for matching one state with another.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

lessonCopy.example.steps.0: For ψ_+, the plus overlap is (1/2)+(1/2)=1, so P(+)=1.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: For ψ_-, the same overlap is (1/2)−(1/2)=0, so P(+)=0. The original-basis probabilities were still 1/2 and 1/2 for both.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: Multiplying ψ_+ by i gives overlap i and probability |i|²=1. That common phase does not change the plus-outcome prediction.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.0: The overlap is (1+i)/2, whose squared magnitude is 1/2.
lessonCopy.practice.prompt: In basis (u₀,u₁), use normalized coefficients c₀=√3/2 and c₁=i/2. Use u_+=(u₀+u₁)/√2 for the final part.
lessonCopy.practice.parts.2.feedback: The overlap is (√3+i)/(2√2); its squared magnitude is (3+1)/8=1/2.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.0.description: The alternate states are explicitly defined as sums and differences divided by √2.

normalize-one-d.idea: Normalization makes the total position probability equal one.
normalize-one-d.explanation: Keep the wavefunction’s shape, but adjust its overall size. A wavefunction is a rule giving amplitudes at positions; its squared size must add up to one across space.

example.title: Scaling a sine shape
steps: On a 2 m interval, use ψ(x) = A sin(πx/2 m). The integral of the sine squared is 1 m.
Choose A = 1 m⁻¹ᐟ². The total probability is then one.

terms.definition: Scaling a state so its total probability is one.
A rule giving quantum amplitudes at positions.
The multiplier setting the sine wave’s size.
Position within the interval.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
A way of adding many small pieces to find a total. Adding small pieces of distance can give the length of a whole trip.

lessonCopy.check.prompt: If L increases by a factor of 9, how does |A| change?
lessonCopy.apply.answer: No. Multiplication by e^(iα) has magnitude 1, so |ψ|² and its integral stay the same. Multiplying by a real magnitude other than 1 would change normalization unless the coefficient were rescaled again.

interval-probability.idea: Equal-sized regions can have different chances of containing a particle.
interval-probability.explanation: The chance depends on all the density inside the region. Where the density is larger, an equally wide region can collect more probability.

example.title: The left quarter of a box
steps: Use the normalized sine shape √(2/L) sin(πx/L). Its density is low near the ends.
The chance in the left quarter is 1/4 − 1/(2π), about 9.1%, rather than 25%.

terms.definition: How tightly probability is packed into space.
The box length.
Position measured from the left wall.

lessonCopy.body.0: Use the normalized sine state ψ(x)=√(2/L)sin(πx/L) on 0≤x≤L. Its density is ρ(x)=(2/L)sin²(πx/L), largest near the centre and zero at the endpoints.

gaussian-state.idea: A Gaussian state has a smooth, bell-shaped position distribution.
gaussian-state.explanation: The distribution’s width describes the spread of position results. Find this spread from the squared amplitude, called probability density, rather than from the amplitude alone.

example.title: A bell-shaped position distribution
steps: Set the centre at 0.50 m and the standard deviation at 0.20 m.
About 68.27% of position results fall between 0.30 m and 0.70 m.

terms.definition: A smooth bell-shaped distribution.
A measure of how widely results spread around their average.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
Chance per small interval or region. Add the density over a region to find the chance of detecting the particle there.

lessonCopy.body.1: Squaring gives ρ(x)=1/(√(2π)σ) exp[−(x−x₀)²/(2σ²)]. This is the normalized Gaussian probability density with mean x₀ and standard deviation σ. The amplitude and density have different exponents; forgetting the square creates a width error.
lessonCopy.body.2: To check normalization, set u=(x−x₀)/σ. Then dx=σdu, and use the standard Gaussian integral ∫ from −∞ to ∞ exp(−u²/2)du=√(2π). This integral identity is supplied here; it is not an elementary antiderivative. It makes the total density integral exactly 1.
lessonCopy.apply.answer: No. Multiplying this amplitude by a position-dependent phase such as e^(ik₀x) leaves |ψ|² unchanged but shifts the momentum distribution. Here k₀ has units rad/m so k₀x is dimensionless. A common phase is different: it changes neither position nor momentum probabilities.

wavefunction-inner-product.idea: Two overlapping shapes can still have zero quantum overlap.
wavefunction-inner-product.explanation: Quantum overlap adds products of amplitudes, including their signs and phases. Positive and negative contributions can cancel even when both shapes occupy the same region.

example.title: Two sine shapes
steps: Use normalized sine shapes with one and two half-waves across the same interval.
Their product has equal positive and negative contributions. Its integral is zero, so the states are orthogonal.

terms.definition: Having zero quantum overlap.
The same complex number with the imaginary part’s sign reversed.
The two position-amplitude functions.
The complex conjugate of f.
Position.
Add contributions continuously over position.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
A way of adding many small pieces to find a total. Adding small pieces of distance can give the length of a whole trip.

lessonCopy.body.0: For functions on the same position domain, define ⟨u,v⟩=∫u*(x)v(x)dx. Conjugate the first function before multiplying. The integral is a complex overlap amplitude, not the probability of a position interval.
lessonCopy.body.2: For ψ=(u₁+i u₂)/√2, projection gives ⟨u₁,ψ⟩=1/√2 and ⟨u₂,ψ⟩=i/√2. In an ideal measurement with these outcome states, the probabilities are each 1/2. Reversing the inner-product arguments conjugates the result, so keep the order clear.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.1: Correct. Complex conjugation changes i to −i.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.1.description: The first argument is conjugated. Coefficients come from ⟨basis state,ψ⟩.

basis-coefficients.idea: A quantum state can be built from reference states whose measurement outcomes are known.
basis-coefficients.explanation: Each reference state has a number called an amplitude. In an orthonormal basis, each reference state has unit length and zero overlap with every other one. Squaring each amplitude’s size gives the chances for this measurement. If you keep only some outcomes, their chances can add to less than one.

example.title: Keeping two of three parts
steps: Three reference outcomes have probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2.
Keeping the first two retains 0.8 of the weight. Renormalizing gives 0.625 and 0.375 for that selected part.

basis-coefficients.equation: basis coefficient = overlap of the reference state with the prepared state

terms.definition: A complete set of reference states used to describe other states.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
Each reference vector has length one, and different reference vectors have zero overlap.

lessonCopy.body.1: Orthonormality removes cross terms from the total norm, so ⟨ψ,ψ⟩=Σ_j|c_j|². A normalized state has a sum of 1. Individual components are mathematical basis contributions, not a claim that an unmeasured system secretly occupies one particular basis state.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: In a three-state orthonormal basis, choose coefficients √0.5, √0.3 and i√0.2. Their squared sizes sum to 0.5+0.3+0.2=1.

two-state-interference.idea: Two wave contributions can add up strongly or cancel, even when their individual sizes stay fixed.
two-state-interference.explanation: Their phase tells how far each has gone through its cycle. If the phase difference stays predictable, the parts are coherent. Add their amplitudes as numbers that carry both size and phase. Then square the size of the sum to predict a chance.

example.title: Two contributions at one position
steps: The contributions at one point are 0.50 and 0.7071 in units of m⁻¹ᐟ², with matching phase.
Their sum is about 1.2071 m⁻¹ᐟ². Squaring gives density about 1.4571 per metre; adding the separate densities would miss interference.

terms.definition: Having a maintained relative phase.
A change in combined probability caused by adding amplitudes.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

lessonCopy.body.1: Multiplying ψ by its conjugate gives ρ=½u₁²+½u₂²+u₁u₂cosφ. The last part is the interference cross term. It can be positive or negative, but the total density remains nonnegative because it is |ψ|². Its integral over all space is 1 because the cross integral vanishes for orthogonal functions.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: At that position, density is [0.75+(1/√2)cosφ]m⁻¹. For φ=0 it is about 1.4571 m⁻¹; for φ=π it is about 0.04289 m⁻¹.
lessonCopy.apply.answer: No. That is a common phase factor and cancels from |ψ|². Changing only the relative phase of one component changes the cross term; multiplying both together does not.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.1.description: The probability in a region is ∫ρdx, not ρ at one point.

coherent-versus-mixture.idea: Picking a preparation at random differs from combining two waves in a single preparation.
coherent-versus-mixture.explanation: If a coin chooses one of two preparations, average their predicted chances using the coin’s probabilities. If the two parts belong to one wave and keep a definite phase relationship, their amplitudes can add or cancel. That difference can show up on the meter.

example.title: A half-and-half mixture
steps: Prepare u₀ on half the runs and u₁ on the others. Each gives the plus outcome with probability 1/2.
The mixture’s plus chance is ½ × ½ + ½ × ½ = ½.

coherent-versus-mixture.equation: outcome chance = sum of (preparation weight × conditional chance)

terms.definition: An ensemble described by probabilities for different prepared states.
Two orthogonal normalized reference states.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
Individual outcomes can vary even when you repeat the same setup.

lessonCopy.body.1: Both preparations give probabilities 1/2 and 1/2 in the original (u₀,u₁) measurement. But their alternate-basis statistics differ. The plus outcome u_+=(u₀+u₁)/√2 occurs with probability 1 for preparation A.

projective-update.idea: An ideal measurement that gives a particular result leaves only the part of the state matching that result.
projective-update.explanation: Think of the measurement as a filter for the possible readings. After one reading is recorded, keep its wave part and rescale it so its total chance is one. Repeat the same ideal test straight away, with no other change, and you get the same reading.

example.title: Recording outcome one
steps: Prepare (3/5)u₀ + (4/5)u₁. Outcome one has chance 16/25.
If one is recorded, keep (4/5)u₁ and normalize it. The new state is u₁.

projective-update.equation: updated state = selected component / its length

terms.definition: Keeping the part of a state belonging to a chosen outcome.
Normalized states belonging to the two distinct outcomes.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

schrodinger-one-d.idea: A rule called the Schrödinger equation predicts how a particle’s wave changes with time.
schrodinger-one-d.explanation: A wavefunction assigns a wave amplitude to each position. To predict the next wave, the rule uses the current shape and the potential energy at each place. You also need a starting shape and rules for the edges, such as where a wall forces the wave to be zero.

example.title: Change at one point
steps: Suppose the curvature term is zero at a point and the potential energy is 3.0 × 10⁻²¹ J.
There the amplitude changes at rate −i(V/ℏ)ψ. This local rule is not a complete state by itself.

schrodinger-one-d.equation: iℏ × time-change rate = −(ℏ²/2m) × spatial curvature + Vψ

terms.definition: Energy associated with the system’s position or arrangement.
The position amplitude.
Potential energy at the point.
Particle mass.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
The imaginary unit.
How the amplitude’s slope changes with position.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

hamiltonian-action.idea: A wave can have one definite energy, or it can contain several possible energies.
hamiltonian-action.explanation: The energy operator is a mathematical rule that acts on the wave. For a wave of definite energy, this rule multiplies every part by the same energy value. The shape stays in the same proportion everywhere. Most wave shapes do not pass that single-energy test.

example.title: Testing one Gaussian shape
steps: For a free Gaussian shape, applying the energy operator gives a multiplier that depends on position.
At its centre the multiplier is E₀; at one width away it is zero. The state therefore has no single definite energy.

hamiltonian-action.equation: energy rule applied to a definite-energy state = energy × same state

terms.definition: A mathematical rule acting on a state.
The operator representing energy.
The positive energy scale for this Gaussian example.

separate-time.idea: A state with one definite energy can have an unchanging pattern of likely positions.
separate-time.explanation: When the energy rule stays fixed, the whole wave advances through its cycle together. This shared phase changes the wave numbers but leaves all their sizes unchanged. Squaring those sizes to predict positions therefore gives the same pattern later.

example.title: One changing phase
steps: An energy state gains the time factor −i at a chosen time.
Since |−i|² = 1, multiplying the amplitude by −i leaves its density unchanged.

terms.definition: The alignment of an amplitude; a common phase leaves probabilities unchanged.
The imaginary unit, with |i| = 1.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

evolve-superposition.idea: Parts of a wave with different energies can move out of step with one another.
evolve-superposition.explanation: At first the parts might reinforce each other on the left. Later their different rates can make them reinforce on the right. This can change where a particle is likely to be found while its chances of giving each energy reading stay the same.

example.title: Two equally weighted energies
steps: Prepare the equal plus combination of two energy states separated by ΔE.
At t = πℏ/ΔE, their relative sign has reversed. The chance of the original plus outcome is now zero.

terms.definition: A state formed by adding amplitudes of reference states.
Energy difference between the two states.
Elapsed time.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.

probability-current.idea: Probability in a region changes when more flows in than out.
probability-current.explanation: Probability current describes this flow rate. It keeps track of chances crossing a boundary; it does not assign a hidden path to each particle.

example.title: Flow through an interval
steps: The left boundary has incoming current 0.30 per second. The right has outgoing current 0.10 per second.
The region’s probability is increasing at 0.20 per second at that instant.

probability-current.equation: probability change per second = incoming current − outgoing current

terms.definition: The rate of probability flow through a boundary.

position-momentum-actions.idea: Position and momentum ask different questions about the same wave.
position-momentum-actions.explanation: To apply the position rule, multiply the wave’s value at each point by its position x. For momentum, first find the wave’s slope at each point. Multiply that slope by −iℏ. Here i² = −1 and ℏ is the fixed constant that sets the quantum scale.

example.title: A plane-wave factor
steps: For the factor e^(ikx), taking the derivative gives ik times the same factor.
Multiplying by −iℏ leaves ℏk times the original factor: its momentum value is ℏk.

position-momentum-actions.equation: momentum of the plane-wave factor = ℏk

terms.definition: A rule describing how quickly a quantity changes.
Wave number: phase change per unit distance.
Position.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
The imaginary unit.
A complex phase with angle kx.

operator-domains.idea: A quantum rule needs boundary rules for the input waves it allows.
operator-domains.explanation: A formula alone does not specify every allowed wave. On a ring, going once around returns to the same point, so the wave must join itself there. This is one needed boundary check, not a complete proof that a measurement rule is valid.

example.title: Joining a wave around a ring
steps: Let a ring’s circumference be L. Positions 0 and L name the same point.
The amplitude must therefore have the same value at both ends: ψ(0) = ψ(L). A trial with unequal values fails this boundary check.

terms.definition: The wave’s position amplitude.
The ring’s circumference.
The allowed input waves, including their boundary rules.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

expectation-variance.idea: A predicted average need not be a possible single result.
expectation-variance.explanation: Multiply each outcome by its chance, then add. This gives the average over many matching preparations; the spread describes how much individual results vary.

example.title: Two possible energies
steps: Energy is 2E₀ with chance 3/4, or 6E₀ with chance 1/4.
The average is 3E₀, although no single result can be 3E₀ in this model.

expectation-variance.equation: predicted average = sum of (outcome × its probability)

terms.definition: The predicted average over repeated matching preparations.
A fixed positive energy unit.

commutator-action.idea: Doing two quantum operations in a different order can change the result.
commutator-action.explanation: A commutator measures the difference between the two orders. In a product such as AB, apply B first, then A; use only inputs for which both orders are allowed.

example.title: Two small matrices
steps: Let A swap two entries and B reverse the second entry’s sign. Start with (1,0).
AB gives (0,1), but BA gives (0,−1). Their difference is (0,2).

terms.definition: The difference between applying two operations in opposite orders.

ehrenfest-motion.idea: The average motion of many identically prepared particles can follow familiar force rules.
ehrenfest-motion.explanation: The average force sets how fast the average momentum changes in this model. If the force bends sharply with position, different parts of the wave feel different forces. Averaging those forces need not give the force at the average position.

example.title: A free particle’s average motion
steps: A particle has mass 2.0 × 10⁻³⁰ kg and average momentum 6.0 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s.
Its average position changes at 3.0 × 10⁵ m/s.

ehrenfest-motion.equation: average-position change per second = average momentum / mass

position-momentum-spread.idea: Spread describes how widely repeated measurement results vary.
position-momentum-spread.explanation: Prepare matching copies and measure each quantity on a separate group. The state’s spread is different from a detector’s resolution; a coarse readout describes only what that detector reports.

example.title: A two-bin readout
steps: A detector reports −2 nm or +2 nm with equal chances.
The average readout is zero and its standard deviation is 2 nm. This is the readout’s spread, not a complete continuous position distribution.

position-momentum-spread.equation: standard deviation = √(average squared distance from the mean)

terms.definition: A measure of how widely results spread around their average.

gaussian-momentum.idea: Squeezing a bell-shaped wave into a narrower region makes its range of possible momenta wider.
gaussian-momentum.explanation: A Gaussian is a smooth bell shape. Use the standard deviation, a measure of spread, for both the position readings and the momentum readings. For the simple wave here their product stays at ℏ/2. Narrow one spread and the other must grow.

example.title: A narrow Gaussian
steps: The position standard deviation is 0.50 nm.
Its momentum standard deviation is ℏ/(1.00 nm), about 1.055 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s.

terms.definition: A smooth bell-shaped distribution.
A measure of spread around the average.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.

robertson-bound.idea: The spreads of position and momentum cannot both be made as small as we like in a single prepared state.
robertson-bound.explanation: Imagine measuring position on one group of identical preparations and momentum on another. Use the standard deviation of each group as its spread. For the allowed states here, multiplying the two spreads gives at least ℏ/2, where ℏ sets the quantum scale.

example.title: A specified position spread
steps: Let the position standard deviation be 0.80 nm.
The momentum standard deviation must be at least ℏ/(1.60 nm), about 6.59 × 10⁻²⁶ kg·m/s.

terms.definition: A measure of how widely results spread around the average.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.

uncertainty-interpretation.idea: Squeezing a particle’s wave can raise its average kinetic energy even when its average momentum is zero.
uncertainty-interpretation.explanation: Start with the bell-shaped free-particle wave in this lesson. A narrower position pattern gives a wider spread of momentum. Positive and negative momenta can cancel in the mean. Their squares enter kinetic energy and add together instead.

example.title: Halving the prepared width
steps: For mass 2.0 × 10⁻³⁰ kg, a zero-mean Gaussian of width 0.50 nm has average motion energy about 2.78 × 10⁻²¹ J.
Halving its width multiplies that energy by four, to about 1.11 × 10⁻²⁰ J.

uncertainty-interpretation.equation: average motion energy = ℏ² / (8 × mass × position spread²)

terms.definition: A smooth bell-shaped state.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.

spatial-curvature.idea: The local energy difference helps determine whether a particle’s wave repeats or fades.
spatial-curvature.explanation: In a region where potential energy stays fixed, compare it with the total energy. Above the potential energy, the wave can bend back and forth through cycles. Below it, the allowed shapes grow or shrink by repeated factors. Conditions at the edges decide which shape fits.

example.title: A decaying part
steps: Suppose the decay constant is 2/L. Moving a distance L reduces the chosen amplitude by e⁻².
Its density falls by the square of that factor: e⁻⁴, about 0.0183.

terms.definition: How the slope of a shape changes.
A chosen positive length.
The number about 2.718 used for exponential change.
How fast an exponential amplitude shrinks with distance.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

boundary-matching.idea: When the potential energy jumps by a finite amount, the wave must join correctly on both sides.
boundary-matching.explanation: Picture drawing the wave from left to right across a step. For the constant mass and ordinary finite step used here, there can be no gap in the drawing and no sudden corner. Both the wave’s height and its slope must agree at the join.

example.title: Joining two solutions
steps: At the boundary, matching requires A + B = C and A − B = 2C.
Solving gives A = 1.5C and B = −0.5C. A negative amplitude contribution is allowed; probability uses the squared total size.

terms.definition: The place where two regions meet.
Amplitude coefficients for the waves being joined.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
How much a graph rises or falls for each step to the right.

parity-bound-states.idea: A mirror-symmetric trap can have waves that follow simple mirror rules.
parity-bound-states.explanation: A bound state stays confined near the trap. For the smooth one-dimensional trap here, an energy wave is even if its value stays the same when left and right are swapped. It is odd if each value changes sign. This lets one side help determine the other.

example.title: An odd shape
steps: Take g(x) = C(x/L)e^(−x²/2L²). Its centre value is zero.
At x = L and x = −L, the amplitudes have opposite signs but equal densities.

terms.definition: A state’s even or odd reflection rule.
Position relative to the center.
A positive length scale.
A multiplier setting the amplitude’s size.
The number about 2.718 used for exponential change.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

shooting-check.idea: A trial energy is useful only if its wave fits at both ends of the model.
shooting-check.explanation: Start at one edge, use the guessed energy to calculate the wave step by step, and compare the far end with the required value. The difference is called the residual. Repeat with smaller calculation steps to check whether a close match was only a numerical accident.

example.title: Finding the first box level
steps: Trials at scaled energies 8 and 12 miss the endpoint with opposite signs, so a root lies between them.
Refining the calculation approaches 9.8696044, or π². A tiny endpoint miss alone would not prove that accuracy.

shooting-check.equation: endpoint miss = calculated amplitude at the far boundary

terms.definition: The remaining mismatch after a trial calculation.
Energy divided by the model’s fixed energy unit.

infinite-well-spectrum.idea: Two impenetrable walls allow only certain standing-wave shapes.
infinite-well-spectrum.explanation: The amplitude must be zero at both ends. Only a whole number of half-waves fits, so the allowed energies form a separated list; the everywhere-zero shape is not a state.

example.title: The first box energy
steps: Let ℏ²/(2mL²) = 0.020 eV. For the first allowed shape, n = 1.
Its energy is π² × 0.020 eV, about 0.19739 eV.

infinite-well-spectrum.equation: allowed box energy = n²π² × energy scale

terms.definition: A wave pattern with fixed zero-amplitude points.
The positive whole-number level label.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
Particle mass.
Box length.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

well-normalization-probability.idea: A region’s probability comes from adding the density inside it.
well-normalization-probability.explanation: For the box’s lowest-energy sine shape, the density is smaller near the walls. A quarter of the width therefore need not contain a quarter of the probability.

example.title: The box’s left quarter
steps: Choose a box 2 nm wide and look in its leftmost 0.50 nm.
For its lowest-energy state, the probability is 1/4 − 1/(2π), about 9.08%.

terms.definition: Probability packed into each unit of position.

well-means-spreads.idea: An average momentum of zero can still go with positive kinetic energy.
well-means-spreads.explanation: A reading of +p and an equally likely reading of −p average to zero. Both give the same positive squared momentum. Kinetic energy uses that square, so the energy contributions add. Here the momentum test describes an ideal release of the particle from the box.

example.title: Releasing one box ground state
steps: Use a 2 nm box with energy scale 0.020 eV. Its ground state has zero average release momentum.
The momentum-square average remains positive, giving motion energy π² × 0.020 eV, about 0.19739 eV. Zero mean momentum does not make that energy zero.

well-means-spreads.equation: average motion energy = average of (momentum²) / (2 × mass)

terms.definition: A state with the lowest allowed energy.

well-superposition-time.idea: Combining two energy states of a particle in a box can make the pattern of likely positions shift back and forth.
well-superposition-time.explanation: Here the box has walls that the particle cannot cross. Each energy state has a wave pattern. When we combine two states, their waves advance through their cycles at different rates. They can reinforce each other on the left now and on the right later. The chance of measuring either energy stays the same.

example.title: Probability in the left half
steps: Prepare equal amplitudes of the first two box states with matching initial phase.
Initially the left-half probability is about 92.44%. Half a pattern cycle later it is about 7.56%.

terms.definition: The relative alignment of amplitudes.
The gap between the two box energies.
Elapsed time.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

periodic-ring.idea: A ring joins the ends instead of placing walls there.
periodic-ring.explanation: The amplitude and its slope must return to their starting values after one turn. Clockwise and counterclockwise states can have the same energy; a constant zero-momentum state is also allowed.

example.title: Two directions around one ring
steps: Let the ring energy scale ℏ²/(2mC²) be 0.010 eV.
The n = +1 and n = −1 states both have energy about 0.39478 eV, despite opposite momentum directions.

terms.definition: A rule joining values after one complete turn.
The integer winding label, positive, zero or negative.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
Particle mass.
Ring circumference.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
How much a graph rises or falls for each step to the right.

finite-well-regions.idea: A particle trapped by a finite energy well can still be detected a little outside it.
finite-well-regions.explanation: A well is a region of lower potential energy. Inside it, a bound wave can form repeating shapes. Beyond either edge its tail shrinks farther from the well. In a stationary bound state the outside chance stays fixed in time.

example.title: A trial outside tail
steps: The outside potential is four energy units and the trial energy is one unit. The model’s length scale is a.
The outside decay length is a/√3, about 0.577a. Matching at the edges must still decide whether this trial energy is allowed.

finite-well-regions.equation: decay length = a/√3 for this trial

terms.definition: A state confined near a region with normalizable decaying tails.
Half the well width in this model.
Distance over which the decaying amplitude falls by a factor e, about 2.718.

finite-well-matching.idea: Only certain energies give a wave that fits inside the well and joins both outside tails.
finite-well-matching.explanation: Try a possible energy and draw its inside and outside waves. At a finite edge the height and slope must match. Check both edges. A wave that looks reasonable in the middle can still fail at one of the joins.

example.title: Testing an even shape
steps: For depth parameter 2 and trial parameter 1, the two matching sides are about 1.557 and 1.732.
They disagree, so this trial is not an allowed energy.

terms.definition: The inside wave number.
Half the well width.
The outside decay constant.
How much a graph rises or falls for each step to the right.

finite-well-roots.idea: We can find an allowed energy by repeatedly halving a range of trial values.
finite-well-roots.explanation: First find a continuous part of the matching rule where its value changes sign. Zero lies between opposite signs if the rule stays continuous there. Test the middle and keep the half that still brackets zero. A jump in the graph can change sign without ever passing through zero.

example.title: Halving a bracket
steps: Start with a valid matching bracket of width 0.1.
After ten halvings its width is 0.1/2¹⁰, about 0.00009766.

terms.definition: The number of bisection steps.
A continuous interval whose endpoint mismatches have opposite signs.

finite-well-tail-probability.idea: An energy well’s outside tails count when adding up the chance of finding the particle.
finite-well-tail-probability.explanation: The total chance over all positions must be one. Add the density inside the well and in both fading tails outside before setting the wave’s overall size. A fixed outside chance in a stationary state does not mean the particle steadily leaks out.

example.title: Counting both tails
steps: For the stated lowest even state, the middle contributes 1.428615 and the two tails contribute 0.154659 to the unnormalized density integral.
Outside probability is 0.154659 divided by their sum, about 9.77%.

finite-well-tail-probability.equation: outside probability = outside density integral / total density integral

terms.definition: A continuous sum over the chosen region.

flux-coefficients.idea: To find how much of a wave gets past a step, compare the incoming and outgoing flows.
flux-coefficients.explanation: Probability flow measures how much detection probability passes a point per second. It depends on both the size of the wave and its speed. If the transmitted wave travels more slowly, squaring its amplitude ratio alone gives the wrong passing fraction. Multiply by the outgoing-to-incoming speed ratio as well.

example.title: A slower transmitted wave
steps: The outgoing-to-incoming wave-number ratio is 1/2, and the amplitude ratio is 4/3.
Transmission is (1/2) × (4/3)² = 8/9.

terms.definition: The transmitted fraction of incoming flow.
The outgoing-to-incoming wave-number ratio.
The transmitted-to-incident amplitude ratio.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

step-above.idea: A quantum wave can partly reflect from a step even when its energy is high enough to continue.
step-above.explanation: Across a sudden change of potential energy, the wave on one side must join the height and slope on the other. A reflected wave helps make both joins fit. Count the outgoing and incoming flows to find how much passes.

example.title: Crossing a step
steps: The incoming and outgoing wave numbers are 4 and 2 per nanometre.
Reflection amplitude is (4 − 2)/(4 + 2) = 1/3, giving reflected fraction 1/9.

terms.definition: Reflected amplitude divided by incoming amplitude.
Wave numbers before and after the step.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
How much a graph rises or falls for each step to the right.

step-below.idea: A wave can reach partway into a high energy step without carrying a steady flow through it.
step-below.explanation: Imagine the higher potential energy continues without end. With lower total energy, the physical wave fades as you move farther into the step. It gives some chance of detecting the particle just inside, while its net flow through this stationary tail is zero.

example.title: A decaying stationary tail
steps: The incoming wave number and decay constant are both 2 per nanometre. The matched outside tail is stationary.
At 0.50 nm beyond the step, density is about 0.2707 times the incoming density, but the net current there is zero.

barrier-below.idea: A barrier of finite width can let some of a quantum wave through even when the wave energy is below its top.
barrier-below.explanation: The wave must fit at the near edge and the far edge. That takes a combination of two mathematical shapes inside the barrier, one that grows and one that shrinks toward the right. Matching them lets us find the wave on the far side.

example.title: A finite rectangular barrier
steps: Choose the stated scales so the barrier width times its decay constant is 1 and its height is twice the incident energy.
The exact transmitted fraction is 1/[1 + sinh²(1)], about 0.420.

terms.definition: The hyperbolic sine: (eᵘ − e⁻ᵘ)/2.
The transmitted fraction of incoming flow.
The number about 2.718 used for exponential change.

barrier-above.idea: Reflections inside a barrier can cancel at certain phases.
barrier-above.explanation: For the ideal rectangular barrier, matching both edges gives full transmission at special wavelengths. This is a phase condition, not a claim that every wave above the barrier passes completely.

example.title: One transmission resonance
steps: Choose an interior wave number q and barrier width d so qd = π.
Then sin²(qd) = 0 and the exact transmitted fraction is one.

terms.definition: Wave number inside the barrier.
Barrier width.
Transmitted flow fraction.
Any positive whole number.
The distance along a wave from one point to the matching point in the next cycle, such as crest to crest.

scattering-packets.idea: A wave packet can contain several energies. Each can have a different chance of getting past a barrier.
scattering-packets.explanation: A wave packet is a wave concentrated in a limited region. To predict how much will get through, find the passing fraction for each energy. Multiply each fraction by that energy’s share of the incoming packet and add the results. This comparison applies after the outgoing packets have separated.

example.title: Two narrow energy groups
steps: Three quarters of the packet has transmission 0.20; one quarter has transmission 0.80.
The total transmitted chance is 0.75 × 0.20 + 0.25 × 0.80 = 0.35.

scattering-packets.equation: transmitted chance = sum of (energy weight × transmission)

oscillator-scales.idea: Two different lengths are useful for a quantum spring. They answer different questions.
oscillator-scales.explanation: The natural length is a convenient ruler built from the mass, the spring’s cycle rate and ℏ. The spread of position readings in the lowest-energy state is a measured-width prediction. Its standard deviation equals that ruler length divided by √2.

example.title: A two-nanometre oscillator length
steps: Let the natural length ℓ be 2 nm.
The ground-state position spread is 2/√2 nm, about 1.414 nm.

terms.definition: The natural length scale for the chosen oscillator.
A measure of how spread out readings are around their average. A larger value means more spread.

oscillator-ground.idea: Even the lowest allowed energy of an ideal quantum spring is above zero.
oscillator-ground.explanation: The lowest wave is bell shaped. Confining the wave means its momentum readings have a spread, so it keeps some kinetic energy. Its position spread also contributes spring energy. Together they give the lowest allowed total.

example.title: The lowest oscillator energy
steps: The oscillator’s energy spacing ℏω is 0.040 eV.
Its ground energy is half that spacing: 0.020 eV.

terms.definition: The lowest oscillator energy.
The energy spacing between neighboring oscillator levels.

oscillator-excited.idea: The first excited oscillator state has one zero-amplitude point.
oscillator-excited.explanation: That point is a node. The amplitude changes sign there, while its squared size remains nonnegative everywhere; a negative amplitude is not a negative probability.

example.title: The centre node
steps: The first excited shape is the ground shape multiplied by √2 x/ℓ.
At the centre x = 0, its amplitude and position density are both zero.

terms.definition: Ground and first excited amplitudes.
The oscillator’s natural length.
A point where amplitude is zero.
Position measured from the trap center.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

oscillator-ladders.idea: Two mathematical rules let us step between the separate energy levels of a quantum spring.
oscillator-ladders.explanation: One rule raises the level by one. The other lowers it by one and multiplies the wave by a known factor. Try lowering the lowest level and the rule gives zero. This signals that there is no next state below it.

example.title: Lowering level two
steps: Apply the lowering operator to normalized state |2⟩.
The result is √2|1⟩. The √2 factor records its size; the output is not automatically normalized.

terms.definition: The lowering operator.
A normalized oscillator state with level number n.
A mathematical rule that acts on a state or function to give another state or function.

oscillator-observables.idea: An oscillator state predicts a distribution, not an imagined orbit.
oscillator-observables.explanation: Even when average position is zero, position results can spread widely around it. Calculate the spread for the prepared state rather than treating the average as every result.

example.title: The first excited state
steps: For level n = 1 and natural length ℓ = 2 nm, the position spread is ℓ√(n + 1/2).
This gives 2√1.5 nm, about 2.449 nm, despite zero mean position.

terms.definition: Position standard deviation.
The oscillator’s natural length.
The oscillator energy-level number.

momentum-representation.idea: One wave can be described by where a particle may be found or by what momentum a meter may read.
momentum-representation.explanation: A Fourier transform rewrites a position wave as a collection of momentum waves. It changes the labels used in the calculation. Square the sizes of the momentum amplitudes and add over the chosen range to get the chance of a reading in that range.

example.title: A uniform momentum window
steps: Momentum is uniformly distributed from 2 × 10⁻²⁴ to 4 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s.
The central half of that interval contains half the probability.

momentum-representation.equation: momentum-interval chance = integral of momentum density over that interval

terms.definition: A rule that rewrites a wave in terms of its momentum components.
A continuous sum over the chosen interval.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

lessonCopy.body.1: Both representations are normalized:∫|ψ|²dx=∫|φ|²dp=1. This norm-preserving Fourier property is Parseval’s identity for the stated convention. Since dp has momentum units, φ has units (kg·m/s)⁻¹ᐟ², not the inverse-square-root-length units of ψ.
lessonCopy.body.2: The momentum mean is ⟨p⟩=∫p|φ(p)|²dp. Probability comes from integrating the spectral density over a momentum interval. A peak in that density does not make every individual momentum measurement equal to the peak value.

free-gaussian-evolution.idea: A bell-shaped wave can spread out over time even with no force pushing its centre.
free-gaussian-evolution.explanation: A packet is a wave gathered in a region. Its different momentum parts advance through their cycles at different rates. The predicted positions then spread over a wider region. For the free packet used here, the distribution of momentum readings stays the same.

example.title: A spreading electron state
steps: Start with width σ₀ = 1 nm and zero average momentum.
At the spreading time t_s, the width becomes √2 nm, about 1.414 nm, while its centre stays fixed.

terms.definition: Initial position standard deviation.
Position standard deviation at elapsed time t.
The time when this packet’s width has grown by a factor √2.

lessonCopy.body.2: Taking the squared magnitude uses |q|=√(1+τ²). The resulting density is Gaussian with centre x_c and width σ_x(t)=σ₀√(1+τ²). The momentum width remains σ_p=ℏ/(2σ₀), because free momentum probabilities do not change. The time t_s=2mσ₀²/ℏ is the scale where the position width grows by √2.

classical-correspondence.idea: Check the relevant scale before treating quantum spreading as negligible.
classical-correspondence.explanation: For a free Gaussian, spreading depends on mass, starting width and elapsed time together. Small spreading does not by itself remove every quantum effect or prove a classical path.

example.title: A specified heavy free state
steps: An ideal 1 g mass starts with position spread 1 micrometre. After 1 second its spreading parameter is about 5.28 × 10⁻²⁰.
Its width change is negligible on this scale. This says nothing about every possible state of a gram-sized object.

terms.definition: Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
Elapsed time.
Mass.
Initial position standard deviation.

lessonCopy.body.1: Mean motion can also look classical: Ehrenfest’s equation gives d⟨p⟩/dt=−⟨V′(x)⟩. Replacing the mean force by −V′(⟨x⟩) needs the force to vary little across the occupied packet, or a force exactly linear in x. A small spreading parameter alone does not justify that separate replacement.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: These are two stated free-state examples, not predictions for every gram-sized object or electron in an environment. For a harmonic potential V=½kx², the force is −kx, so its mean equals −k⟨x⟩ exactly even for a broad state.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.0: The first change in √(1+τ²) is quadratic, not linear in τ.
lessonCopy.practice.parts.1.label: Width for the 2 nm preparation
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.0.description: Positive m and σ₀; the free-width approximation uses |τ| much smaller than 1.

spherical-coordinate-bridge.idea: A point can be located by distance and two angles.
spherical-coordinate-bridge.explanation: Spherical coordinates use distance from the centre, angle from the upward axis, and angle around that axis. A small cell grows wider farther from the centre, which matters when adding volumes.

example.title: Locating one point
steps: Go 2 m from the origin, turn 90° from the upward z-axis, and choose zero angle around it.
The point is (2,0,0) m on the positive x-axis.

spherical-coordinate-bridge.equation: x = r sinθ cosφ; y = r sinθ sinφ; z = r cosθ

terms.definition: Distance from the origin.
Angle from the positive z-axis.
Angle around the z-axis measured from positive x toward positive y.
The usual three perpendicular position coordinates.

lessonCopy.example.steps.0: At r=2 m, θ=π/2 and φ=0, the Cartesian point is (2,0,0) m.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: Near that point, dr=0.10 m, dθ=0.10 rad and dφ=0.20 rad give a small-cell volume approximately (2 m)²×1×0.10 m×0.10×0.20=0.0080 m³.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.1.description: θ is from +z; φ is around z from +x toward +y.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.2.description: dΩ=sinθdθdφ; integrating over all directions gives 4π.

three-d-probability.idea: A thin outer shell contains more space than an equally thick inner shell.
three-d-probability.explanation: To find a radius probability, include the shell’s volume as well as the density at each point. Radius density and volume density therefore answer different questions.

example.title: A uniform ball
steps: Imagine uniform probability per volume inside a ball of radius 2 m.
The inner ball of radius 1 m has only 1/8 of the volume, so it contains 1/8 of the probability.

lessonCopy.body.0: In three dimensions, probability is ∫|ψ(r)|²dV. The normalized wavefunction has units m⁻³ᐟ² and the density has units m⁻³. These differ from the one-dimensional units because the integration measure is volume.
lessonCopy.body.1: For a spherically symmetric state, density depends only on r. Integrating over directions gives the radial probability density P_r(r)=4πr²|ψ(r)|². Then probability between radii a andb is ∫ₐᵇP_r(r)dr. P_r has units m⁻¹ and is not the same function as the volume density.
lessonCopy.body.2: For a simple probability example, take constant amplitude A inside a ball of radius R and zero outside. Normalization gives |A|²[4πR³/3]=1, so radial density inside is 3r²/R³. This sharp boundary is a probability example only; it is not automatically a finite-kinetic-energy or stationary state for an ordinary smooth Hamiltonian.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: The probability inside r=R/2 is the volume fraction (R/2)³/R³=1/8, not 1/2. The outside region from R/2 toR contains the remaining 7/8.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.1: Correct. The inner volume fraction is (1/4)³=1/64.

orbital-lz.idea: Knowing angular momentum along one direction does not tell us where the particle is around its axis.
orbital-lz.explanation: The z direction is one chosen axis. A quantum wave can give a definite angular-momentum reading along z while being spread equally all the way around it. The reading describes how the wave responds to rotation, rather than picking an angle for the particle.

example.title: An angular phase with label two
steps: Use angular factor e^(2iφ)/√(2π). Its z-angular-momentum value is 2ℏ.
Its angular density is uniform, so any quarter-turn interval has probability 1/4.

terms.definition: The integer angular label, not mass.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
Angle around the z-axis.
The measured z-component of orbital angular momentum.
The imaginary unit.
A complex phase factor with angle 2φ.

lessonCopy.body.1: An azimuthal factor Φ_m(φ)=e^(imφ)/√(2π) is an eigenfunction because differentiating gives ∂Φ_m/∂φ=imΦ_m, and then L̂_zΦ_m=mℏΦ_m. The integer label m is a quantum number here, not mass.
lessonCopy.body.2: Single-valued orbital scalar states must return to the same value after φ increases by 2π. Since e^(i2πm)=1, this azimuthal label is an integer. The factor Φ_m is normalized over φ, but it is only an angular factor, not by itself a complete admissible three-dimensional wavefunction at the polar axes.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: For m=2, differentiating Φ₂ gives 2iΦ₂. Multiplication by −iℏ gives L̂_zΦ₂=2ℏΦ₂.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: The density |Φ₂|² is 1/(2π), so the azimuth probability in a π/2-wide interval is 1/4. Definite L_z does not select one azimuth direction.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.meaning: Differentiate the azimuthal phase and multiply by −iℏ. A phase that winds an integer number of times around the axis gives a definite orbital z-component mℏ.

orbital-joint-states.idea: A zero angular-momentum reading along z does not require zero total angular momentum.
orbital-joint-states.explanation: The z reading measures one component along a chosen axis. The total size uses all directions. Quantum states can have definite values for the total size squared and one component together. That does not assign definite values to all three components at once.

example.title: An orbital state with ℓ = 1, m = 0
steps: Its z-component is mℏ = 0.
Its total angular-momentum square is ℓ(ℓ + 1)ℏ² = 2ℏ², so the total is not zero.

terms.definition: The total orbital angular-momentum label.
The label for one chosen component.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
The measured squared total orbital angular momentum.
The measured component along z.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

lessonCopy.body.0: Orbital operators obey [L̂_x,L̂_y]=iℏL̂_z and cyclic counterparts. The total square L̂²=L̂_x²+L̂_y²+L̂_z² commutes with L̂_z. That permits common eigenstates with L² eigenvalue ℏ²ℓ(ℓ+1) and L_z eigenvalue mℏ.
lessonCopy.body.1: For scalar orbital states, ℓ is a nonnegative integer and m runs through −ℓ,−ℓ+1,…,ℓ. The square-root scale √[ℓ(ℓ+1)]ℏ is the magnitude associated with L², not the same number as a measured z-component. Do not draw it as a classical vector with all components simultaneously known.
lessonCopy.body.3: To verify the last statement, the spherical angular operator is L̂²=−ℏ²[(1/sinθ)∂_θ(sinθ∂_θ)+(1/sin²θ)∂_φ²]. Acting on Ccosθ gives 2ℏ²Ccosθ: the φ derivative vanishes, and the θ derivatives produce −2Ccosθ inside the brackets. C is the stated normalization coefficient.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: For ℓ=1, the L² eigenvalue is 2ℏ² and the allowed L_z values are −ℏ,0,+ℏ. There are three m labels.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: The state Y₁₀=Ccosθ has ∂_φY=0. Also ∂_θY=−Csinθ, so (1/sinθ)∂_θ(sinθ∂_θY)=−2Ccosθ; hence L̂²Y=2ℏ²Y.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.1.description: ℓ=0,1,2,… and −ℓ≤m≤ℓ. These m labels are not masses.

central-radial-equation.idea: If potential energy depends only on distance from the centre, we can study distance and direction separately.
central-radial-equation.explanation: Choose a wave pattern for the directions around the centre. What remains is a rule for how the wave changes with radius. Angular momentum adds a positive energy term to this radial rule when it is nonzero. It does not describe a little orbit.

example.title: The extra radial term
steps: For orbital label ℓ = 1, the extra term is twice ℏ²/(2μr²).
At the stated mass and radius 1 nm, it is about 0.0763 eV.

terms.definition: Orbital angular-momentum label.
The mass used for relative motion.
Distance from the centre.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
Electronvolt, an energy unit often used for atoms.

lessonCopy.body.0: A central potential depends only on r, so write a stationary state as ψ(r,θ,φ)=R(r)Y_ℓm(θ,φ). Normalize Y over solid angle. Then the radial normalization is ∫₀∞|R|²r²dr=1, without an extra 4π because Y already accounts for the directions.
lessonCopy.body.1: The spherical Laplacian can be written∇²=(1/r²)∂_r(r²∂_r)−L̂²/(ℏ²r²). It is the 3D second-derivative operator expressed in spherical coordinates. Substituting the separated state into the stationary Schrödinger equation replaces L̂² by its eigenvalue ℏ²ℓ(ℓ+1).
lessonCopy.body.2: Set u(r)=rR(r). The first-derivative radial terms simplify, giving −(ℏ²/(2μ))u″+[V(r)+ℏ²ℓ(ℓ+1)/(2μr²)]u=Eu. Here μ is the particle or reduced mass, and a prime means derivative with respect to r. The radial norm becomes ∫₀∞|u|²dr=1.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: For a mass μ≈9.11×10⁻³¹ kg at r=1.0 nm and rounded ℏ=1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s, the scale ℏ²/(2μr²)≈6.109×10⁻²¹ J≈0.03813 eV.

radial-boundaries.idea: A candidate wave around an atom needs to behave properly at the nucleus and far away.
radial-boundaries.explanation: Radial means measured outward from the centre. Multiply the radial wave by its distance from the centre. For the ordinary potentials and the electric attraction considered here, this product must approach zero at the centre. A bound state’s far tail must fade as well.

example.title: Checking one candidate
steps: Take u(r) = Nr e^(−r/a), with positive length a. It vanishes at r = 0 and decays at large r.
Its physical radial factor u/r stays finite at the centre. The full energy equation still needs checking.

radial-boundaries.equation: u(0) = 0 for the stated allowed radial solutions

terms.definition: Radius times the radial part of the wavefunction.
Distance from the centre.
A normalization constant.
A positive decay length.

lessonCopy.practice.parts.3.label: Total radial norm ∫|u|²dr
lessonCopy.practice.parts.3.feedback: The stated normalized Y and u give total probability 1, with no extra 4π.

hydrogen-reduced-mass.idea: Both the proton and electron move inside hydrogen.
hydrogen-reduced-mass.explanation: Separate the atom’s overall motion from the motion between its two particles. The internal calculation uses a reduced mass, which accounts for both moving instead of fixing the proton in place.

example.title: A finite proton mass
steps: If the proton is 1836 times as massive as the electron, the reduced mass is 1836/1837 of the electron mass.
It is slightly smaller, giving a slightly larger atomic length scale than the fixed-proton model.

terms.definition: Reduced mass for relative motion.
Electron mass and proton mass.

hydrogen-ground.idea: The most likely radius differs from the point of greatest density.
hydrogen-ground.explanation: Hydrogen’s ground-state density per volume is greatest at the centre. But larger-radius shells contain more volume, so the radius distribution peaks away from the centre; neither describes an orbit.

example.title: Probability inside one atomic length
steps: The ground state’s radius distribution peaks at r = a.
The probability inside that radius is 1 − 5e⁻², about 32.33%; a peak does not mean most results lie inside it.

terms.definition: Electron-proton separation.
The ground-state Coulomb length scale.
The exponential constant, about 2.718.
A state with the lowest allowed energy.

hydrogen-spectrum.idea: In the simple hydrogen model, a bound electron can have only certain energies.
hydrogen-spectrum.explanation: A bound electron stays near the proton. Its wave must fit near the centre and fade far away. Only certain waves with whole-number labels satisfy both conditions. Several shapes can have the same energy in this model.

example.title: Hydrogen’s second energy family
steps: With the rounded energy scale 13.6 eV, label n = 2 gives −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV.
Four spatial states share that energy when spin and additional corrections are left out.

terms.definition: Positive integer energy-family label.
The positive Coulomb binding-energy scale.
The energy of the family labeled n.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

hydrogen-nodes.idea: A node is a place where the amplitude is zero.
hydrogen-nodes.explanation: The node can be a sphere or a plane, depending on the state’s shape. The amplitude may change sign across it, while density remains nonnegative because we square the amplitude’s size.

example.title: The hydrogen 2s node
steps: The 2s radial amplitude contains the factor 2 − r/a.
At r = 2a this factor is zero, creating a spherical node.

terms.definition: Electron-proton separation.
The Coulomb length scale.
The hydrogen state with principal label 2 and orbital label 0.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

hydrogen-transition-energy.idea: When an atom moves to a lower energy level it can give the lost energy to one photon.
hydrogen-transition-energy.explanation: A photon is a packet of light. The difference between the two levels gives its energy and frequency in the model here, which neglects the atom’s recoil. Matching energies is one test. The way light interacts with the two states must also allow the change.

example.title: The allowed 3p to 2s transition
steps: Using the rounded 13.6 eV scale, the energy drop is 13.6(1/4 − 1/9), about 1.8889 eV.
The photon’s vacuum wavelength is about 1240/1.8889 = 656.47 nm.

hydrogen-transition-energy.equation: photon energy = initial atomic energy − final atomic energy

terms.definition: Nanometre: one billionth of a metre.
One packet of electromagnetic radiation. Visible light and radio waves can both be described in photons.
For a repeating signal, the number of cycles per second. Five cycles each second is 5 hertz.
The distance along a wave from one point to the matching point in the next cycle, such as crest to crest.

quantum1-model-choice.idea: First identify what the meter counts. Different kinds of readings need different wave calculations.
quantum1-model-choice.explanation: For one separate outcome, square the size of its amplitude. For a range of positions, add the probability density across the range. For a steady stream meeting a barrier, compare the outgoing flow with the incoming flow to find the passing fraction.

example.title: A scattering measurement
steps: Incoming probability current is 6 per second and transmitted current is 4 per second.
The transmitted fraction is 4/6 = 2/3. An amplitude without its speed information would not settle that fraction.

terms.definition: The rate of probability flow through a boundary.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

quantum1-bound-capstone.idea: Position chances can change while energy chances stay fixed.
quantum1-bound-capstone.explanation: In a fixed box, an equal combination of two energies keeps their weights. Their relative phase changes with time, so interference changes the chance of a later position result if no measurement interrupts the evolution.

example.title: A two-energy box state
steps: Prepare equal amplitudes of energies 0.20 and 0.80 eV. The initial left-half chance is about 92.44%.
A quarter of the pattern’s cycle later, it is 50%, while both energy chances remain 50%.

terms.definition: The relative time phase between the two energy components.
Pi, about 3.142.
Probability of finding the particle in the left half.
Wave contributions can strengthen or cancel when they meet. Quantum amplitudes can do this, too.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

quantum1-scattering-capstone.idea: A bigger wave on the far side of a step can still carry a smaller flow of probability.
quantum1-scattering-capstone.explanation: Flow counts how much chance passes a point per second. A transmitted wave moving slowly can carry less flow than a faster incoming wave, even if its height is larger. Include the speed ratio as well as the squared height ratio when comparing the flows.

example.title: A four-electronvolt incident state
steps: Total energy is 4 eV and the step is 3 eV, giving a wave-number ratio of 1/2.
The amplitude ratio is 4/3, so transmission is (1/2)(4/3)² = 8/9.

terms.definition: Transmission fraction.
Outgoing-to-incoming wave-number ratio.
Relative transmitted amplitude, not time.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
One amount divided by another. Three red counters for every two blue gives a red-to-blue ratio of 3/2.

quantum1-assessment.idea: Check what an average tells you before treating it as an individual outcome.
quantum1-assessment.explanation: State the allowed results and their chances, then calculate their average. Explain the answer in words and name the preparation assumptions; a correct number alone does not show every quantum topic is understood.

example.title: A fresh energy distribution
steps: Energy is 1 eV with chance 3/4 and 5 eV with chance 1/4.
The mean is 2 eV. The variance is 3 eV², giving a spread √3 eV.

quantum1-assessment.equation: variance = mean of squared results − square of mean

terms.definition: The average squared distance of results from their mean.
Something you take as true for a calculation, such as assuming that a cart’s speed stays steady.
